To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the 13-cis retinoic acid (isotretinoin) trial of the Head and Neck Intergroup was a landmark study of chemoprevention for second primary tumors (recurrence) and that the genetic analysis of the trial has identified genetic markers that can be used to predict who is likely to benefit from the treatment, as well as who is likely to develop a second primary tumor.

(i) the 13-cis retinoic acid (RA) treatment effect on second primary tumor (SPT) prevention in head-and-neck cancer patients was modified by genetic polymorphisms of the retinoic acid receptor (RAR) and retinoid X receptors (RXR) genes, and (ii) the RAR and RXR gene polymorphisms identified in this study may be used for individualized SPT risk assessment.

(a) a genetic variant of the retinoblastoma tumor suppressor gene (RB1) is associated with a higher risk of second primary cancers (SPC) among head and neck cancer survivors, and (b) this variant is associated with a lower risk of SPC among head and neck survivors who received the chemopreventive agent isotretinoin (13-cis retinoic acid; 13-cRA) compared with placebo.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new generation of cancer prevention strategies that are personalized to the individual patient.
the identification of genetic factors that influence cancer susceptibility.
the identification and validation of biomarkers that predict response to cancer prevention interventions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the 13-cis-RA trial, as originally designed and executed, was a failure.
the results of the current study suggest that the use of 13-cRA for the prevention of SPT or recurrence in patients with head-and-neck cancer should be based on the patient's genotype status.

this study has identified a number of SNP markers that are predictive of response to 13-cRA treatment and that these markers are associated with risk of recurrence or SPT in patients treated with placebo.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
this study has demonstrated the importance of genetic variation in cancer prevention and that this approach can be applied in the future to the design of cancer-prevention trials.
the genetic information we have identified can be used for individualizing the prevention of second primary tumors in patients with head and neck cancers.
the genetic variation in a population of patients with cancer can help identify those patients at highest risk of recurrence or new cancers, and those most likely to benefit from preventive therapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are many genetic variations that are important in determining the risk of cancer.
there are some people who are at higher risk of getting a second cancer and some who are at lower risk.
the use of genotypes in a risk assessment for SPTs or recurrence of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) can be used to personalize cancer prevention.
